analysis.one_liner: Requires permits and cleanup plans for sewer overflows polluting coastal waters, with federal help paying for the work.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 28 cosponsors from both parties and a joint hearing in June 1990, but it never received a House vote and died in committee when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to write permit rules for overflows from combined storm water and sanitary sewer systems that discharge into estuaries, oceans, and the Great Lakes. Sewer operators would have had to spend money to identify and eliminate dry-weather overflows and minimize wet-weather ones by the end of 1999, with federal grants and technical assistance to help pay. It would also have tightened permits for any discharge into coastal waters, requiring applicants to prove the discharge is needed, monitor it, and accept that the permit can be changed or ended to protect the water.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use coastal beaches and waters, since the bill's own findings state that combined sewer overflows are a primary source of beach degradation and a major reason for beach closures along the North Atlantic coast [S3]. Coastal residents, commercial and sport fishermen, and the tourism economy would gain from cleaner water. Local sewer systems would benefit from federal grants, technical assistance, and flexible permit rules [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to issue permit rules for combined sewer overflows discharging into estuarine zones, coastal waters, and the Great Lakes, bringing a largely uncontrolled source of pollution under the Clean Water Act permit system.

Requires each permit holder to budget and spend money to identify all overflows, put technology-based limits in place, and eliminate the discharges, with a goal of ending dry-weather overflows and minimizing wet-weather overflows by the end of 1999.

Makes federal cleanup grants available to permit holders and directs the EPA to give technical assistance to state and local governments, recognizing in its findings that coastal state and local governments cannot afford the fix on their own.

Bars new or renewed permits for discharges into estuaries and oceans unless the applicant proves the discharge is needed, there is no environmentally sound alternative, and ongoing monitoring is in place, and prohibits waiving these requirements.

Directs the EPA to identify estuaries where sewer overflows are a major pollution source, push for priority action plans there, and report to Congress on the extent of the problem and the federal cost of fixing it.

analysis.who_pays: Local governments that operate combined sewer systems would bear the compliance costs, which the bill itself estimates in the billions of dollars, likely passed on to sewer ratepayers and local taxpayers; federal taxpayers would fund the authorized grants. Entities discharging pollutants into oceans and estuaries would face stricter permit tests and monitoring costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Local sewer systems, their ratepayers, and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings put the cost of eliminating combined sewer overflows in the billions of dollars, and the burden would fall on local sewer systems and their ratepayers; the bill authorizes federal grants at 'such sums as are necessary' but appropriations are never guaranteed.

The mandatory expenditure requirement would force permit holders to budget and spend set amounts as a condition of their permits, a real strain for cash-strapped cities, though the EPA could waive it for systems with a credible cleanup plan in place.

Title III's requirement that applicants prove no environmentally sound alternative exists could block or delay some ocean and estuary discharges outright, imposing costs on the entities that currently rely on those discharges.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are genuinely large — the bill itself concedes a multi-billion-dollar price tag that local governments say they cannot afford — but the bill is built to soften the blow: federal grants, technical assistance, flexible system-wide permits, and waivers for communities with credible cleanup plans. The benefit side is concrete: cleaner beaches, protected fisheries, and an end to untreated sewage overflows into coastal waters by 2000. This is an expensive but reasonably designed approach to a problem the record describes as a primary cause of North Atlantic beach closures. The honest caveat is that the federal money was authorized, not guaranteed, so ratepayers could have been left holding much of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and their subcommittees; one day of joint hearings was held in June 1990, but the bill was never brought to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Thomas Manton of New York, joined by Rep. Norman Lent, introduced the bill on August 3, 1989, and it was referred jointly to the Public Works and Transportation Committee and the Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee.

It was then split among subcommittees on Water Resources, Oceanography and Great Lakes, and Fisheries and Wildlife Conservation and the Environment, with the EPA, OMB, and Commerce asked for their views.
The bill attracted 28 cosponsors, 20 House Democrats and 8 House Republicans, and the subcommittees held a joint hearing on June 20, 1990.
No committee ever reported the bill and it never reached the House floor; the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill still pending in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo prevailed: combined sewer systems and other ocean dischargers avoided multi-billion-dollar cleanup obligations, while beach communities, fishermen, and coastal residents got no relief from the overflows and closures the bill was written to fix.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Dischargers and sewer systems; no cleanup

for.name: Rep. Thomas J. Manton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require permits and cleanup of combined sewer overflows into coastal waters.

for.name: Rep. Norman F. Lent
for.what_they_did: Joined Manton in introducing the bill, giving it Republican sponsorship from the start.

for.name: Subcommittees on Oceanography and Great Lakes and on Fisheries and Wildlife Conservation
for.role: House Merchant Marine and Fisheries subcommittees
for.what_they_did: Held a joint hearing on the bill on June 20, 1990.

against.name: House Committee on Public Works and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on August 3, 1989 and never reported it out; its Water Resources subcommittee took no recorded action after referral.

against.name: House Committee on Merchant Marine and Fisheries
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on August 3, 1989; its subcommittees held one hearing but the full committee never reported the bill.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor in the roughly 16 months between its hearing and the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Democratic sponsor with a Republican co-introducer and 28 cosponsors split 20 Democrats to 8 Republicans — but the bill never reached a vote, so no record shows how the chambers would have divided.

industries.industry: Municipal sewer and wastewater utilities (largely city and regional governments)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed multi-billion-dollar obligations to identify and eliminate overflows, but paired them with federal grants, technical assistance, flexible system-wide permits, and waivers for communities with credible cleanup plans — help these systems themselves said they needed.

industries.industry: Water infrastructure construction and engineering firms
industries.note: Mandated spending on overflow identification, technology upgrades, and system corrections would have translated into major contracts, paid for largely by federal grants and local budgets.

industries.industry: Coastal tourism, beach communities, and commercial and sport fishing
industries.note: The bill targeted the overflows it identified as a primary cause of beach degradation and North Atlantic beach closures, directly protecting the waters these industries and communities depend on.

industries.industry: Industrial and municipal dischargers into oceans and estuaries
industries.note: Title III would have required them to prove no environmentally sound alternative exists, fund ongoing monitoring, and accept permits that regulators could modify or terminate, with no waivers available.
